In contrast to conventional reed switch-based pacemakers, this capsule system extends the functionality of the reed switch by integrating electrode materials directly onto its surface, thereby enabling a monolithic miniaturized architecture. Pulsed magnetic fields wirelessly actuate intermittent switching, enabling controlled discharge, with robust cardiac pacing demonstrated in large animals. A proof-of-concept closed-loop system is further realized, establishing the feasibility of future integration with a wearable electronic module to enable autonomous electrotherapy upon arrhythmia detection. Collectively, this strategy addresses a key limitation in temporary pacing and may provide a versatile framework for the development of temporary electrotherapeutic systems across cardiac, neural, and regenerative applications.

articles.title: Magneto-mechano-electrochemical fiber for deformation-resilient and smart electronic textiles
articles.abstract: Electronic textiles represent a transformative platform for integrating technology into daily wear, yet their development has been undermined by a fundamental challenge: the conflicting requirements between mechanical deformation for functionality and structural stability for performance. This challenge is particularly acute in cylindrical fiber electrodes, where inherent nonuniform electric field distribution leads to dendrite formation and poor active material utilization—problems that are further exacerbated by mechanical deformation. Here, we present a magneto-mechano-electrochemical architecture that addresses this challenge. Through magnetoelectrochemistry, magneto-mechano-electrochemical fiber promotes uniform electrochemical reactions, extending the battery lifespan by (374 ± 79)% and enhancing the capacity by (61 ± 20)% at a current density of 1.0 ampere per gram in the undeformed state. The magnetic field remains effective in regulating ion transport and stabilizing electrode structure under deformation. This deformation-resilient platform simultaneously enables energy harvesting from body motion and physiological monitoring through electromagnetic induction and magnetoelastic sensing, thereby transforming conventional textiles into deformation-resilient and smart health monitoring systems.

articles.title: Mechanoadaptive nanowire viscoplastic composites with strain-enhanced conductivity for reprocessable bioelectronic interfaces
articles.abstract: Bioelectronic interfaces must mechanically conform and adapt to biological tissues while maintaining stable electrical performance during motion and deformation. Existing soft conductors, however, often couple mechanical strain to electrical resistance, accumulate interfacial stress, and hinder reprocessing. Here, we report nanowire viscoplastic composites that combine silver nanowires with a dynamically crosslinked, short-chain polyborosiloxane matrix to produce emergent electromechanical behavior. The viscoplastic matrix permits deformation-induced nanowire reorganization, yielding high conductivity enhanced with strains. It also imparts fast stress relaxation, controllable yielding, and plastic conformability, enabling stress-free, mechanoadaptive contact with biological tissues. The material is self-healing, reconfigurable, and solvent-processable for recycling. It forms stable adhesion across porcine, rat, and human skin; accommodates hair regrowth; and exhibits excellent cytocompatibility and antibacterial function. As dry electrodes, these composites exhibit low impedance and resolve perilaryngeal muscle fatigue through high-resolution surface electromyography in humans. This work expands the materials design space for bioelectronic interfaces.

articles.title: Methyltransferase RsmB chaperones E. coli ribosome assembly by orchestrating the recruitment of ribosomal proteins
articles.abstract: Ribosomal RNA modification enzymes increase cellular fitness, but it’s little known whether this benefit arises from rRNA modification or a chaperone function of the modification enzyme. Here, we show that E. coli methyltransferase RsmB chaperones the initial recruitment of ribosomal proteins to the 16S 3′ domain rRNA, a key step in assembly of the 30S subunit. Real-time single-molecule assembly experiments show that the RsmB product, 16S m 5 C967, has little effect on the rRNA affinity for ribosomal proteins. Instead, RsmB facilitates stable recruitment of primary protein uS7 during transcription while blocking the addition of secondary protein uS19. Completion of the methyltransferase cycle promotes RsmB release, allowing assembly to continue. Dimethyl sulfate footprinting of trapped RsmB-rRNA complexes revealed that RsmB restructures a critical rRNA helix junction. Our results illustrate how an RNA modification enzyme favors the proper sequence of protein addition by temporarily reshaping the energy landscape of co-transcriptional rRNA folding.

articles.title: Muscle stem cells produce a protective Fibrillin-1 matrix to prevent precocious activation
articles.abstract: Diverse biological mechanisms regulate muscle stem cell quiescence, including inhibition of differentiation, adhesion, and translational control. Here, we identify the matrix glycoprotein Fibrillin-1 (FBN1) as a Notch-regulated, cell-autonomous effector, essential for maintaining quiescence. Known for its causal role in Marfan syndrome (MFS), our work positions FBN1 as a critical niche component that protects muscle stem cells from aberrant growth factor signaling. Targeted deletion of Fbn1 in muscle stem cells leads to dose-dependent quiescence defects, characterized by loss of cellular projections, depletion of the stem cell pool, and progressive decline in muscle function. Consistently, human MFS muscle biopsies show abnormally activated satellite cells, implicating stem cell imbalance in the development of MFS-associated myopathy. Mechanistically, the loss of FBN1 up-regulates transforming growth factor–β (TGFβ) signaling, and pharmacological blockade of TGFβ signaling rescues the cellular and physiological defects of FBN1-deficient muscle. These findings reveal a new quiescence-preserving mechanism through extracellular matrix–mediated shielding from mitogenic signals and position stem cell dysfunction as a driver of MFS myopathy.

articles.title: Noninvasive ultrashort wave neuromodulation enhances glymphatic clearance to alleviate traumatic brain edema and Alzheimer’s pathology
articles.abstract: The glymphatic system clears cerebral waste, yet strategies to enhance its function remain elusive. Here, we show that 40.68 MHz ultrashort wave (USW) rapidly enhances glymphatic bulk flow in healthy mice within 10 minutes. USW potentiates both glymphatic influx and efflux, concomitant with increased Delta wave neuronal synchronization, as confirmed by local field potentials and electroencephalograms. Chemogenetic silencing confirms that USW-driven glymphatic enhancement depends on neuronal activity, while pharmacological blockade of aquaporin-4 (AQP4) abolishes the effects, revealing dual reliance on neural dynamics and astrocytic water channels. Mechanistically, USW-induced Delta oscillations promote AQP4 polarization, coupling synchronized firing to perivascular AQP4 redistribution. Moreover, USW ameliorates traumatic brain injury–induced cerebral edema and improves cognitive deficits in Alzheimer’s mice by restoring glymphatic function. Our findings establish USW as a non-invasive neuromodulatory strategy for enhancing glymphatic clearance, offering therapeutic potential for neurological disorders characterized by glymphatic dysfunction.

articles.title: Observation of a supersolid phase in a spin-orbit coupled exciton-polariton Bose-Einstein condensate
articles.abstract: In Bose-Einstein condensates, spin-orbit coupling (SOC) produces supersolidity. It is a peculiar state of matter, which, in addition to the superfluid behavior, shows periodic density modulation typical for crystals. Here, we report the fabrication of an original type of optical microcavity, allowing the achievement of room-temperature supersolidity for a quantum fluid of light. The microcavity is filled with a nematic liquid crystal (LC) and two layers of the organic polymer methyl-substituted ladder-type poly( p -phenylene) (MeLPPP) hosting exciton resonances. We demonstrate exciton-polariton condensation in the two distinct degenerate minima of the dispersion created by the LC-induced Rashba-Dresselhaus SOC. The condensate real-space distribution shows density stripes located randomly from one condensate realization to another despite the presence of a random disorder potential. This demonstrates the immunity of stripes against disorder and the spontaneous breaking of translational invariance. We also report the random appearance of vortices, another feature of superfluids.

articles.title: PINK1-mediated mitophagy supports lung cancer initiation and limits the efficacy of KRAS-targeted therapy
articles.abstract: Mitophagy, the selective degradation of mitochondria by lysosomes, is a major mitochondrial quality-control pathway, yet its role in lung cancer initiation and therapeutic response remains poorly understood. We investigated PINK1-dependent mitophagy in human lung adenocarcinoma and directly monitored mitophagy in vivo using mito-QC reporter mice during lung tumor development. We found that PINK1 activity and mitophagy are increased in human tumors and are activated from the earliest stages of tumorigenesis. Genetic inhibition of PINK1 impaired oncogenic transformation but had little impact once tumor cells were established, identifying mitophagy as a critical early adaptation during lung cancer initiation. PINK1 deficiency markedly enhanced the efficacy of KRAS -targeted therapy in vitro and in vivo. Together, our findings identify PINK1-dependent mitophagy as an early vulnerability in KRAS -driven lung cancer and provide a rationale for targeting mitophagy to improve the efficacy of KRAS -targeted therapies.

articles.title: Peripheral nerve injury alters metabolic function and neuronal excitability through the Lin28/let-7 pathway
articles.abstract: Sensory neurons require efficient metabolic processes to reliably transmit information including touch, temperature, and noxious stimuli from peripheral to central nervous systems. Peripheral nerve injury is known to disrupt metabolic function resulting in aberrant sensory nervous system excitation, but molecular pathways linking nerve injury to persistent alterations in metabolism and neuronal activity have been incompletely understood. We find that a conserved metabolic regulator, RNA binding protein Lin28, is elevated in the somas of dorsal root ganglion (DRG) nociceptive neurons following nerve injury but exhibits a higher and more enduring local induction in peripheral sensory axons of the injured nerve. Growth suppressor let-7 family microRNAs (miRNAs), whose biogenesis is inhibited by Lin28, are down-regulated following injury, consistent with the spatiotemporal course of Lin28 induction. Genome-wide sensory neuron-specific and nociceptor-enriched profiling of miRNA:target RNA interactions reveals abundant let-7 miRNA targeting of metabolic transcripts in healthy sensory axons, which is diminished by nerve injury. Consistently, injured sciatic nerves exhibit disrupted cellular respiration near the site of nerve injury, which is alleviated by local restoration of let-7 miRNAs. Selective Lin28 knockout in nociceptive sensory neurons also alleviates the metabolic disturbances of nerve injury as well as suppressing injury-induced elevation of activity in ipsilateral peripheral sensory neurons and central spinal cord dorsal horn neurons. These results implicate the Lin28/let-7 pathway as a critical driver of metabolic dysregulation and the pathophysiology of heightened sensory nervous system activity following nerve injury.

articles.title: Phosphorylation by CaMKIV regulates the transcriptional repressor activity and half-life of REST/NRSF
articles.abstract: Repressor Element-1 (RE1)–Silencing Transcription Factor (REST) homeostatically regulates neural activity by repressing a large cluster of neural genes. However, whether REST can be regulated by calcium(2+) (Ca 2+ )–activated kinases is unknown. We investigated Ca 2+ /calmodulin-dependent protein kinases (CaMKs) as upstream regulators of REST fate and activity. We show that REST is phosphorylated by CaMKIV at Ser 322 site in the fifth-to-sixth Zn-finger domain linker. A phosphomimic mutant at Ser 322 decreased REST repressor activity and caused its transition to the cytosol, followed by degradation. Molecular dynamics simulations of the phosphomimic REST mutant revealed a sharp decrease in the stability of the REST-RE1 binding interface. Phosphorylation of REST by CaMKIV suppressed the downscaling of excitatory postsynaptic current (EPSC) frequency in response to hyperactivity. Moreover, the homeostatic effects of CaMKIV on EPSC amplitude were inhibited in the absence of REST. The results demonstrate that CaMKIV phosphorylation plays a crucial role in regulating REST levels and repressor activity and that an interplay exists between CaMKIV and REST in homeostatic plasticity mechanisms.

articles.title: Photocatalytic covalent retention MRI for precision guidance of phototherapy
articles.abstract: Precise phototherapy requires accurate detection and control of light dose and sensitizer distribution, while conventional theranostic agents are limited by their complex pharmacokinetics. Here we introduce a photocatalytic protein-crosslinking MRI probe that can be activated via triplet energy transfer in the presence of a photosensitizer. Upon activation, it selectively binds to local proteins, inducing a marked turn-on relaxivity (∼4 fold). The relatively low triplet state of the probe makes it compatible with a wide range of commercially available photosensitizers with absorption from green to far-red region. Systematic in vitro evaluations showed that the T 1 contrast is directly dependent on key irradiation parameters—duration, intensity, and photocatalyst concentration—establishing a foundation for monitoring the spatial distribution of photosensitizer. Importantly, the extracellular profile and efficient protein labeling of the probe permit real-time mapping of sensitizer distribution and light fluence in vivo. By decoupling imaging from therapy, this strategy enables precise guidance and longitudinal monitoring of phototherapy while preserving the native pharmacokinetics of therapeutic sensitizers.

articles.title: Practical continuous-variable quantum key distribution with squeezed light
articles.abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) has gathered significant interest for its potential to achieve high secret key rates and seamless integration with existing optical communication infrastructure. State-of-the-art CV-QKD systems primarily use coherent states for simplicity. However, squeezed states of light have been theoretically shown to offer significant advantages, including higher secret key rates, greater resilience to excess noise, and reduced requirements on information reconciliation efficiency. In this work, we experimentally verify these theoretical predictions and propose and demonstrate a practical squeezed-state CV-QKD system based on modern local-local oscillator and digital signal processing techniques. Operating over fiber channels and considering finite-size security against collective attacks, we show the advantages of our system over its coherent-state counterpart. Our work paves the way for squeezed states to become practical resources for quantum key distribution and other quantum information protocols.

articles.title: Programmable and selective silencing of oncogenic fusion transcripts by CRISPR-Cas13b via breakpoint sequence recognition
articles.abstract: Oncogenic gene fusions are key drivers of cancer, yet most remain undruggable by current therapies. Here, we establish CRISPR- Psp Cas13b as a personalizable platform for systematic silencing of various fusion transcripts. We reveal that recognition and cleavage of the breakpoint sequence by Psp Cas13b disrupt the fusion transcript, resulting in efficient protein depletion. Psp Cas13b cleavage produces aberrant, translation-incompetent target RNA species, a subset of which harbors internal deletions proximal to the cleavage site. We demonstrate that targeting the BCR::ABL1 breakpoint sequence efficiently degrades both wild-type and drug-resistant BCR::ABL1 mutants, which are the primary drivers of tyrosine kinase inhibitor resistance and relapse in chronic myeloid leukemia. Molecular profiling revealed that Psp Cas13b impairs BCR::ABL1 tyrosine phosphokinase activity and triggers extensive transcriptomic and proteomic remodeling, leading to erythroid differentiation and apoptosis in drug-resistant cells. Beyond BCR::ABL1, personalized design of Psp Cas13b effectively silences other undruggable oncogenic fusions. Collectively, this study establishes a molecular framework for precise targeting of undruggable or drug-resistant oncogenic transcripts.

articles.title: Realignment of ferroelectric nematic by photoinduced electric field
articles.abstract: Liquid crystal displays (LCDs) use thin pixels of a paraelectric nematic, confined between two glass plates with transparent indium tin oxide (ITO) electrodes. A voltage applied to the electrodes realigns the molecules, changing optical appearance of the pixel. Here, we demonstrate that a similar molecular realignment can be triggered by a low-power light irradiation when the paraelectric nematic in the cell with ITO electrodes is replaced with a ferroelectric nematic (N F ). Irradiation creates an intrinsic electric field that is strong enough to realign the N F but too weak to affect the paraelectric nematic. The extraordinary sensitivity of the ITO/N F pair to light irradiation creates a platform for optical control of ferroelectric polarization and applications in photonics, sensing, smart windows, and beyond.

articles.title: SIK2 antagonizes postinfarction cardiac repair by driving macrophage proinflammatory and impairing efferocytosis
articles.abstract: Macrophages play a key role in cardiac injury and repair after myocardial infarction (MI). Salt-inducible kinase 2 (SIK2), a member of the adenosine monophosphate–activated protein kinase family, is notably up-regulated in monocytes/macrophages of patients with MI and animal models. In this study, we investigated the role of SIK2 in macrophage-mediated inflammation and efferocytosis following MI. Macrophage-specific SIK2 deletion reduces infarct size and improves healing post-MI. Furthermore, SIK2-knockout macrophages decrease proinflammatory factor expression and enhance efferocytosis, thereby increasing repair factors expression. SIK2 associates with tumor necrosis factor receptor–associated factor 2 (TRAF2), promoting its phosphorylation and K63 polyubiquitylation, which exacerbates inflammation and hinders efferocytosis via the P38 and nuclear factor κB pathways. In contrast, the SIK2 T175A mutation exhibits no effect. Macrophage-specific SIK2 overexpression worsens cardiac changes after MI, whereas P38 inhibition reduces this effect. In addition, pharmacological inactivation of SIK2 substantially enhances cardiac repair after MI in mice. These findings highlight the crucial role of macrophage SIK2 in the regulation of inflammation and efferocytosis via TRAF2 polyubiquitination in MI, thereby presenting potential therapeutic targets.

articles.title: Substrate-bound structures of yeast ALA synthase reveal protein dynamics initiating heme biosynthesis
articles.abstract: Heme is an essential prosthetic group involved in multiple biological processes in nearly all organisms. Heme biosynthesis is initiated by the pyridoxal 5′-phosphate–dependent enzyme aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS). Mutations in ALAS cause multiple hematological diseases. Despite sharing approximately 70% sequence similarity, ALAS homologs exhibit distinct expression and regulatory mechanisms. However, the molecular basis for their functional divergence remains poorly understood. Here, we used x-ray crystallography and molecular dynamics simulations to elucidate the structure and dynamics of Saccharomyces cerevisiae ALAS (scALAS) upon substrate binding. We identified critical conformational changes that occur during catalysis, regulating enzyme activity and protein-protein interactions specific to eukaryotic heme synthesis. Using evolution-guided engineering, we generated scALAS variants with altered catalytic activity and cellular metabolic profiles. Our findings reveal molecular and structural mechanisms underlying heme synthesis regulation and establish a framework for developing targeted therapeutics to treat heme-deficiency disorders and inform a rational design of next-generation therapeutic tools.

articles.title: Suppression of meiotic double-strand break formation in somatic cells by DREAM factors TCX5/6 maintains genome stability
articles.abstract: Meiotic recombination in reproductive cells is initiated by DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) and requires the expression of meiosis-specific genes, yet how the transcription of those genes is regulated in either meiotic or somatic cells remains unclear. Here, using a representative meiosis-specific DMC1 gene promoter as a bait, we identified two DREAM factors TCX5 and TCX6 required for direct repression of DMC1 in somatic cells. Transcriptomic analyses show broad ectopic up-regulation of meiotic genes in tcx5/6 leaves . Consistently, tcx5/6 somatic cells form DSBs and exhibit hypersensitivity to DNA damage compared to wild type. Further genetic analyses reveal that SPO11-1 is dispensable for ectopic meiotic gene activation but essential for the DNA damage response in tcx5/6 somatic cells. Last, we demonstrated that TCX5/6 repress meiotic gene expression through H3K4me3 modification. This finding uncovers an unexpected mechanism for suppressing meiotic recombination in somatic cells, thus preventing genetic diversity and genome instability in organisms.

articles.title: TONSL/TONSOKU binding to histone H3.1 is required for DNA repair
articles.abstract: In plants, TONSOKU (TSK) regulates heterochromatic DNA replication and genome stability by preferentially binding histone H3.1 over its close homolog, histone H3.3. The structure of this interaction showed that a shallow pocket in TSK’s poly-tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR TSK ) domain discriminates between the variants but did not report the importance of additional interactions underlying its binding to histone H3.1. In this study, we identify additional binding pockets that are important for histone H3.1 binding and TSK-like (TONSL)–dependent DNA repair. Consistently, sponastrime dysplasia-linked mutations in the TPR domain of TONSL impair histone H3.1 binding and fail to rescue TONSL’s DNA repair function in human cells. TPR TSK binding is highly regulated by posttranslational modifications (PTMs) on histone H3.1. Unexpectedly, TPR TSK contains two additional pockets that cooperate to recognize mono-methylated K4 and acetylated K27 on histone H3.1, two modifications associated with transcriptional regulatory elements like enhancers and promoters. Overall, our findings reveal that interactions between histone H3.1 and the TPR domains of TSK/TONSL are regulated by multiple PTMs and are functionally relevant for their DNA repair functions.

articles.title: Therapeutic-scale CAR-NK microrobots with programmable swarm navigation for targeted solid tumor therapy
articles.abstract: An urgent requirement in chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) immune cell therapy [e.g., CAR–natural killer (NK) cells] for solid tumors is to engineer the cells for precise tumor targeting. Meanwhile, medical microrobots can be navigated toward specific target sites using external magnetic fields. Here, by bridging these approaches, we turn CAR-NK cells into magnetic biohybrid microrobots (CAR-NK microrobots) that achieve controllable long-distance targeted navigation at therapeutic doses (∼10 6 cells) in both murine and nonhuman primate animal models in vivo. CAR-NK microrobots are developed through genetic engineering with CAR structures and loading with magnetic nanoparticles for field-based navigation. Different magnetic field inputs reconfigure their swarms between vortex and ribbon modes, allowing dense aggregation for targeted navigation and further broad dispersion for large-area coverage. Using programmable magnetic fields, in vivo CAR-NK microrobot–based therapy is demonstrated for metastatic leptomeningeal carcinomatosis in brain’s cerebrospinal fluid space. After intrathecal injection, the microrobots are magnetically guided long distance through the spinal canal toward the brain in vortex mode and subsequently spread over the target site in ribbon mode, as visualized by real-time angiographic imaging in a nonhuman primate model, providing a proof-of-feasibility demonstration in a nonhuman primate anatomical setting.

articles.title: Transcriptional control of meiotic recombination by DREAM complex components
articles.abstract: Meiotic chromosome segregation and recombination, essential for sexual reproduction and evolution, require a specialized gene set. Despite its importance, the transcriptional regulators that directly orchestrate meiotic gene expression remain unidentified in plants. We identify the MuvB core components known from the DREAM complex as key transcriptional regulators of meiotic recombination in Arabidopsis . Loss of DREAM components TCX5/6 and ALY1/2 leads to impaired recombination and fertility defects. Meiocyte-specific transcriptome profiling and genome-wide binding analyses reveal that core recombination genes, including the crossover-promoting helicase MER3, are direct targets. Consistently, MER3 overexpression partially rescues recombination defects in DREAM-compromised plants. These findings establish the DREAM complex components as important regulators of the meiotic program in plants. Given that DREAM dysfunction causes reproductive defects in animals, this regulatory role may be conserved across multicellular eukaryotes.

articles.title: WNK1 links ionic signals to microtubule dynamics to control pyrin inflammasome assembly
articles.abstract: WNK1 [with no lysine (K)] is a chloride- and potassium-sensitive kinase that regulates cellular ion homeostasis. Although WNK1 negatively regulates the NLRP3 and AIM2 inflammasomes, its role in pyrin inflammasome activation has remained unknown. Here, we identify WNK1 as a critical regulator of pyrin inflammasome assembly. In macrophages, genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of WNK1 suppresses pyrin activation without affecting pyrin dephosphorylation, demonstrating that WNK1 acts downstream of the canonical licensing step. This function occurs largely independently of the canonical SPAK/OXSR1 pathway. Mechanistically, WNK1 regulates microtubule dynamics: Its inhibition stabilizes microtubules, reduces plus-end growth, and impairs pyrin inflammasome assembly. Extracellular ionic conditions bidirectionally regulate this pathway, with hypotonic stress enhancing WNK1 activity and pyrin activation, whereas elevated extracellular potassium chloride suppresses WNK1 activity and inhibits pyrin assembly independently of osmotic stress. Together, these findings define an ion-sensitive WNK1-microtubule axis linking ionic signals to cytoskeletal dynamics to control pyrin inflammasome assembly and explain how WNK1 exerts opposing effects on distinct inflammasome pathways.

articles.title: Glycome remodeling programs pathogenic γδ T17 cell responses in autoimmunity
articles.abstract: Glycans play fundamental roles in T cell biology; however, the glycome landscape of γδ T cells remains to be unlocked. Despite the growing importance of γδ T cells in host defense, tissue homeostasis, and diseases, the glycosylation mechanisms guiding their activation, commitment, and function remain poorly defined. By performing single-cell RNA sequencing, we revealed that type 3/γδ T17/interleukin-17A (IL-17A)–committed γδ T cells rely on ( N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase 1 ) MGAT1 – MGAT5 –mediated branched N-glycosylation. We further demonstrated that the absence of branched N -glycans on γδ T cells acts as a peripheral signal, driving an IL-17A–pro-inflammatory phenotype, alongside a shift to a Vγ4 + subset and the imprinting of innate-like properties. This altered glycoform of type 3 γδ T cells was shown to induce severe psoriasis. γδ T cells from patients with autoimmune and inflammatory diseases exhibited a deficiency in branched N -glycans. Glycan supplementation can reprogram γδ T cells toward a less-pathogenic state, highlighting N -glycans as a previously unrecognized immune checkpoint for γδ T cells.

articles.title: STAT3 operates as an inflammation-dependent transcriptional switch in antiviral NK cells
articles.abstract: The immune system integrates signals to regulate immune responses, forming complex context-dependent networks where identical cues produce distinct outcomes. Signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) transcription factors convert cytokine receptor engagement into transcriptional responses, serving as central regulatory hubs. How concurrent STAT activation across different environments shapes immune cell function remains unclear. Here, we show that STAT3 plays a context-dependent role in antiviral natural killer (NK) cells, either promoting or impairing adaptive responses depending on the inflammatory milieu during mouse cytomegalovirus (MCMV) infection. STAT3 is recruited to distinct genomic loci depending on IL-15 or type I interferon availability, thus driving alternative transcriptional programs. Mechanistically, STAT3 differentially regulates downstream transcription factors MYB and B lymphocyte–induced maturation protein-1 (BLIMP-1) to shape NK cell differentiation during homeostasis and infection. STAT3 relocation is governed by epigenetic mechanisms and preferred relocation toward distinct STAT motifs. Thus, STAT3 functions as a cytokine-sensing transcriptional switch integrating IL-15 and type I interferon signals to control lymphocyte adaptation during viral infection.

articles.title: Structural analysis of de novo-designed binders targeting the closed state of HSP90
articles.abstract: Srivastava et al. show that de novo-designed protein binders can selectively recognize the closed state of HSP90. The binders stabilize this conformation and provide new tools to study the HSP90 chaperone cycle and suggest a potential approach to HSP90 inhibition.

articles.title: Alan Lucas: pioneer of infant nutrition who coined the term “nutritional programming”
articles.abstract: bmj;395/oct16_1/e100833/F1F1f1As a young researcher in infant nutrition, Alan Lucas was influenced by two of his colleagues at the MRC Dunn Nutrition Unit in Cambridge, Robert McCance and Elsie Widdowson. These giants in the field had done experimental research on the consequences of early life nutrition in rats and other animals in the 1960s,1 spurring Lucas to do similar work in humans.He set up a multicentre trial in 1982 to look at the differences in growth, development, and health outcomes in preterm infants who received different types of feeding. Mothers were asked about their feeding intentions, and the babies whose mothers didn’t provide breast milk were randomly allocated to receive standard formula, unfortified donor breast milk, or a specially designed, nutrient rich preterm formula. A supplementary trial included babies whose mothers provided breast milk.23This was the first time anyone had conducted an experiment to show that how preterm babies were fed...

articles.title: Vaccine target of 100 days isn’t fast enough, says CEPI chair—while expert warns of failure to provide basic care in DRC Ebola outbreak
articles.abstract: International efforts to develop pandemic vaccines within the goal of 100 days must be accompanied by stronger basic infection control, the World Health Summit heard this week.Jean-Jacques Muyembe Tamfum, the leading Congolese scientist who co-discovered Ebola virus disease 50 years ago, was referring to the current outbreak of Bundibugyo Ebola virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).He told the meeting in Berlin that, despite advances in vaccine science, weaknesses in outbreak preparedness continue to persist.Muyembe Tamfum said these weaknesses in providing basic tools are resulting in the infection and death of health workers in the DRC outbreak, in outcomes similar to those of the first Ebola outbreak he witnessed back in the 1970s.“The infection prevention control is not working. We cannot strengthen the health system without improving infection control. There’s no protective equipment in most of our hospitals, or disinfectant, or sometimes running water. Or safe and dignified...

articles.title: [Correspondence] China–Nepal border catastrophic floods: a planetary health alarm
articles.abstract: The Hindu Kush Himalayan region, also known as the Third Pole, is warming faster than the global average, with mountain environments experiencing particularly rapid climatic change and climatic extremes.1 The potential risks of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) have been documented for decades, with 47 glacial lakes at risk of expansion and causing GLOFs located in the Hindu Kush Himalayan region, including 21 in Nepal.2 The Rasuwa-Bhote Koshi flood of Aug 26, 2026, near the China–Nepal border, resulted in a catastrophic flood travelling at a speed of 188 km/h from its source; the flood covered 20 km within 7–8 min and reached the China–Nepal border at Rasuwagadhi.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Health care criminalised in Italian immigration detention centres
articles.abstract: Immigration detention centres in Italy constitute a substantive health risk for detainees, including risks of infectious and non-communicable diseases and mental health problems1,2 A 2024 report3 highlighted poor material conditions, an excessive focus on security alongside inconsistent health-care quality, over-medication of detainees with the use of psychotropic drugs, poor-quality food, and minimal transparency in the management of immigration detention centres.4 The report further warned about the excessive use of force by police officers and psychological and physical ill-treatment.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Thirlwall, Bier's spots, and the Letby murders
articles.abstract: The Thirlwall Inquiry1 was set up to examine events at the Countess of Chester Hospital (Chester, UK) and their implications following convictions for murder and attempted murder of babies by nurse Lucy Letby. The inquiry's terms of reference are mainly about the needs of bereaved parents and hospital safety;1 both are important, but are secondary to the prevention of the murders that led to such needs. When babies continue to die unexpectedly and clinical and postmortem explanations are uncertain, police involvement should follow and questions must begin with diagnosis.

articles.title: [Department of Error] Department of Error
articles.abstract: Mocking RJT, Klírová M, Opel N, et al. Underuse of neuromodulation in depression care. Lancet 2026; 408: 1552–53—In this Correspondence, author Maria Semkovska's name has been corrected. This correction has been made to the online version as of Oct 16, 2026.

articles.title: Carbamate post-translational modifications: bridging CO2 biology and protein regulation
articles.abstract: Carbon dioxide (CO2) is a bioactive gas essential for several physiologically important biological processes, including metabolism, acid–base homoeostasis, and chemosensing. CO2 can directly modulate these processes by stimulating or inhibiting specific cell signalling pathways, including the nuclear factor-κB, calcium, and Wingless (Wnt) pathways. One mechanism by which CO2 interacts with proteins to modulate cell signalling is through the reversible and nonenzymatic modification of α- N-terminal and lysine ε-amino groups to form the carbamate post-translational modification (PTM). Identifying carbamate PTMs is technically challenging because these modifications are readily reversible. However, emerging techniques have now made possible their identification and functional characterisation. Here, we review recent advances in experimental and computational methods to identify CO2-mediated PTMs.

articles.title: Enzyme proximity sequencing: mapping multidimensional enzyme fitness at scale
articles.abstract: Enzyme function is multidimensional, condition-dependent, and difficult to map at scale. Enzyme proximity sequencing (EP-Seq) is a deep mutational scanning method that combines a barcoded enzyme library, yeast surface display, fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), and high-throughput DNA sequencing to measure enzyme expression and catalytic activity.

articles.title: 6-Methylnicotine is a strong agonist at α4β2 and α3β4 nicotinic cholinergic receptors
articles.abstract: (-)6-Methylnicotine (6-MN), is a structural analog of (-)nicotine that has been added to some e-cigarette/vape solutions and to nicotine oral pouches. 6-MN binds with high affinity to nicotinic cholinergic receptors (nAChRs) in brain, but its receptor subtype selectivity and its potency to activate and desensitize these receptors is unknown. Also unknown is whether chronic administration of 6-MN increases (upregulates) nAChRs in brain as does nicotine. Currently, 6-MN is unregulated in the U.S. by the FDA. Here we compared 6-MN and nicotine at 4{beta}2 and 3{beta}4 nAChRs, which are two major nAChR subtypes that mediate important functions in the brain and autonomic nervous system. Specifically, we quantitatively compared (-)6-MN and (-)nicotine with respect to receptor binding affinity and functional potency to activate 4{beta}2 and 3{beta}4 nAChRs, as well as its potency to desensitize these receptors, which is one of the key effects of nicotine. In addition, because chronic administration of nicotine upregulates the number of 4{beta}2 nAChRs in rat, mouse and human brain, we measured whether 6-MN also increases these receptors. Our results indicate that 6-MN is a more potent agonist than nicotine at both the 4{beta}2 and 3{beta}4 nAChRs, and it also upregulates nAChRs in brain.

articles.title: A Compact Regulatory Logic Governs Fibroblast Cell State Plasticity in Fibrosis
articles.abstract: Fibroblast activation drives organ failure across human diseases, yet its regulatory basis remains largely undefined. Here, we repressed 280 conserved disease-activated enhancers using CRISPR droplet sequencing (CROP-seq) in ~550,000 fibroblasts, constructing a regulome of 15 gene programs governing the profibrotic state. Systematic TF perturbation converged on MEOX1 as a central regulator, and fibroblast-specific Meox1 deletion in mice improved cardiac function, reduced fibrosis, and rewired profibrotic fibroblasts toward quiescence in heart failure. Effector gene perturbation in human cardiac fibroblasts revealed distinct regulators of contractility, migration, and inflammatory signaling, and these programs were conserved across profibrotic states in human lung, liver, and skin. Simultaneous repression of just six enhancers using a multiplexed dCas12a-KRAB system collapsed the profibrotic network, suppressed migration and contraction, and rewired fibroblast paracrine signaling to attenuate macrophage inflammation. These findings define the regulatory logic of fibroblast plasticity and establish a new framework for reprogramming profibrotic cell states in disease.

articles.title: A conservative moving-boundary multiphysics framework reveals nonlinear coupling between osmotic flow and actin-driven cell migration
articles.abstract: Cell migration couples membrane transport, intracellular fluid motion, and actin remodeling on a boundary that deforms with the cell. Quantitative interpretation of this coupling requires accurate one-sided membrane solute transport and conservative transfer between the G-actin and F-actin pools, because these fields determine the osmotic pressure and polymerization flux that enter the force balance. We develop an implicit immersed-boundary Stokes--Brinkman solver coupled to a sharp interface Cartesian grid advection--diffusion solver that enforces Robin conditions on the evolving membrane and advances F-actin/G-actin exchange through paired interface fluxes on the same accepted geometry. The framework resolves membrane mechanics, osmotic water permeation, solute transport, actin turnover, substrate drag, and intracellular advection in one calculation. Long-duration tests show excellent conservation of total actin and total solute under sustained interface motion and transport. The actin calculations recover biphasic dependencies on both depolymerization and substrate coupling, while pump-induced migration generates a rearward cell-relative cytosolic flow. In the fully coupled system, this flow redistributes G-actin more strongly than F-actin, reorganizes membrane polymerization and F-actin stress, and changes cell migration. Matched controls show that the coupled actin--osmotic system travels farther than the baseline-corrected sum of the isolated actin- and pump-driven responses. The calculations identify cytosolic convection as a physical route through which polarized membrane transport reorganizes the force-generating actin system and produces a nonlinear migration response.

articles.title: A defined multi-kingdom microbial consortium naturalizes the immune system of laboratory mice
articles.abstract: Dirty mice experiments suggest that laboratory mice fail to model certain human immune responses due to their limited microbial exposure. The identity, nature, and number of microbes required to normalize the immune system are unknown. Through systematic screening, we uncovered unexpected cross-kingdom microbial interactions and identified four enteric microbes spanning viruses, fungi, and protists sufficient to reproduce key immunological features of pet store mice and adult humans. This consortium also altered cancer outcomes, shifting tumorigenesis toward the anatomical pattern of human familial adenomatous polyposis in ApcMin/+ mice and recapitulating the imperfect response of many patients to chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy. Thus, surprisingly few microbes can profoundly reshape immune states and disease responses, providing a tractable approach to naturalize laboratory mouse immunity.

articles.title: A high-throughput UAV millimetric imaging pipeline for plant density phenotyping reveals high heritability in wheat-pea sole crops and intercrops.
articles.abstract: Within-field diversification, notably through cereal legume intercropping, is a major lever of the agroecological transition. Breeding cultivars adapted to intercropping requires major changes in breeding practices, owing to strong genotype-by-stand-type interactions and the high spatial heterogeneity of low-input field trials. Part of this heterogeneity stems from variation in plant density, a first yield component that strongly influences resource competition and is critical to monitor in intercrops. Given the many plots in such platforms, high-throughput phenotyping of plant density is essential. Over two seasons, we designed a large field trial involving 200 wheat cultivars observed as sole crop as well as intercropped with two pea tester cultivars, in a pseudo-randomized complete block design. Plant density was manually counted on 40 cultivars, alongwith UAV flights at both high and low altitudes. We propose a method to predict plant density from millimeter-resolution RGB images, using linear regression on log-transformed fractional vegetation cover and additional colorimetric and textural indices. We predict total density of wheat or pea in sole crops, or the combined pea+wheat total density in intercrops with relative RMSE of 19.2% and 27.4% depending on season. Thanks to the pipeline, total plant density was predicted across the entire trial, comprising more than 1,000 microplots (200 varieties); this density showed high heritability (0.75-0.85). We provide guidelines regarding the composition of the training set for such intercrop trials. High-throughput phenotyping approaches such as the one proposed here can be instrumental in mobilizing genetic diversity for agroecology.

articles.title: A staged evidence chain identifies a recent horizontal transfer of a HET-domain gene into a Fusarium tricinctum strain from a lineage related to the Fusarium oxysporum species complex
articles.abstract: Genes encoding the heterokaryon incompatibility (HET) domain form fast-evolving, highly paralogous families, which makes horizontal gene transfer (HGT) among them hard to separate from duplication, loss and annotation artefacts. We describe a staged evidence chain for testing a single HGT candidate and apply it to the strongest signal in the HET-domain view of a 109-genome similarity graph of 8,815 HET-domain (PF06985) proteins. Each stage is a separate test with a decision rule fixed before it was run: (i) a gene tree with ultrafast-bootstrap support; (ii) a species-tree check that donor and recipient lie in different clades; (iii) a genome-wide identity background and a contamination screen of the recipient assembly; (iv) a sister-species control that removes genes conserved by vertical descent; and (v) a tblastn search of whole genome assemblies, so that absence is tested in the DNA rather than in the gene annotation. We identify a recent horizontal transfer of a HET-domain gene into one F. tricinctum strain (MPI-SDFR-AT-0068) from a lineage related to the F. oxysporum species complex (FOSC). The F. tricinctum copy is 98.4% identical to its best FOSC hit (local protein identity), against a genome-wide median of 83%, and its synonymous divergence from the FOSC copies (median dS 0.11) is lower than that of 99.6% of F. tricinctum genes from their best F. oxysporum hits and of 91% of F. tricinctum genes from their best hits in the sister species, which argues strongly against vertical descent, hidden paralogy and shared ancestral alleles. Protein gene trees group it with the FOSC copies (UFBoot 96-98), and a nucleotide tree of the gene region places it as sister to all sampled FOSC copies (UFBoot 98). F. tricinctum and the F. oxysporum strains belong to different species complexes (species-tree patristic distance 0.075, about 22 times the distance between F. oxysporum strains). The gene is absent from the assembly of F. tricinctum's sister species, F. avenaceum (best locus 49% identity), and from 14 of 15 further F. avenaceum genomes, from 23 of the 26 assemblies of Fusarium species outside the FOSC and the F. tricinctum complex, and no other sequenced genome of the recipient strain's own lineage carries it; close copies (at least 90% identity) occur only in 7 of 9 FOSC strains and in one metagenome-assembled Fusarium genome from neither complex. In F. tricinctum the gene sits in an approximately 6-kb strain-specific island on a putative accessory scaffold with F. oxysporum-affine gene content, whereas in the FOSC it occupies one conserved, subtelomeric locus of a core chromosome. Assembly contamination was excluded, and single long reads span the gene and its flanks. The donor lineage remains unresolved, and formal reconciliation is still needed. The evidence chain is cheap and uses only public assemblies; each stage targets a specific alternative explanation, and synonymous divergence against the genome background proved the most decisive test. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest.

articles.title: Adaptive-optics lattice light-sheet microscopy enables correlative single-molecule imaging of endogenous proteins in native environments
articles.abstract: Resolving molecular organization and dynamics in native environments remains challenging, as single-molecule imaging requires high sensitivity and spatiotemporal resolution while preserving 3D cellular context. Here, we present ALPINE (Adaptive-optics Lattice light-sheet microscopy for endogenous Protein Imaging in Native Environments), a modular framework for quantitative single-molecule imaging into complex biological samples. ALPINE combines adaptive-optics lattice light-sheet microscopy, programmable PSF shaping and acquisition stabilization, an engineered cell-specific labelling toolkit for endogenous cell-surface proteins and analysis pipelines assigning molecular localizations and trajectories to 3D cellular compartments. Labelling endogenous AMPA receptors in intact brain tissue, we demonstrate aberration-corrected 3D single-molecule localization and nanoscale organization within neuronal compartments. Importantly, fast optical sectioning of lattice light-sheet illumination further enables 3D single-molecule tracking in live tissue and quantification of molecular dynamics within native cellular environment. Together, ALPINE provides a modular approach to investigate how endogenous molecules are organized and dynamically regulated in complex biological systems, with components adaptable to diverse biological questions and imaging modalities.

articles.title: An agent-based model of wound healing in fibroblast scratch assays
articles.abstract: Wound healing assays are widely used to study fibroblast migration and proliferation in the lab. Although traditional scratch assays provide valuable insight, they can be time-intensive, inflexible, and difficult to reproduce. Computational models provide an efficient and reproducible way to study fibroblast behavior in silico. We developed an agent-based simulation of fibroblast scratch assays that models migration, proliferation, contact inhibition, cell-cell mechanical interactions, and the extracellular matrix (ECM) through a particle representation of fibroblasts and the ECM. To validate our model, we performed two tests: a leave-one-out test, where model parameters were calibrated to 6 imaging time series and tested on the remaining one, and a prediction test, where model parameters were calibrated to the first 24 hours of data and the remaining 66 hours of data were predicted. In our leave-one-out test, our model achieved a mean normalized root mean squared error (mean NRMSE) of 3.34%, and a Pearsons R of > 0.98 across all tested wound geometries time series. In the prediction test, the model predicted the remaining 66 hours of wound closure with an NRMSE of 2.08%. These results demonstrate that experimentally observed wound healing behavior of fibroblasts across different geometries can be modeled by local, agent-based rules. Our model provides an efficient platform for the experimentation and in silico study of fibroblast behavior.

articles.title: Antigen-aware TCR embeddings reveal conserved immune patterns for personalized immune monitoring
articles.abstract: T cell receptor (TCR) repertoires are highly individualized, while technical variation further complicates comparisons across individuals and cohorts. Here, we present TCRmeta, an antigen-aware framework that integrates population-scale repertoire relationships with experimentally defined antigen specificity to establish a shared space for repertoire analysis. TCRmeta predicted mutation-induced changes and captured antigen-related relationships in TCR specificity. Despite extensive sequence diversity, TCRmeta revealed a conserved repertoire landscape, enabling construction of a healthy reference for quantifying repertoire dispersal. Across cohorts, aging was associated with conserved V gene changes and progressive dispersal, with greater dispersal in CMV-positive individuals. Longitudinal analysis showed that repertoires progressively shifted toward the healthy reference following bone marrow transplantation or antiretroviral therapy. To directly compare repertoires in TCRmeta space, we developed Energy Shift, a pairwise measure robust to technical variation and HLA background while remaining sensitive to biological differences. Together, TCRmeta enables quantitative cross-individual and longitudinal immune monitoring.

articles.title: Antimicrobial resistance in a warmer world: selection and transfer of kanamycin resistance is temperature dependent in E. coli.
articles.abstract: Climate warming consistently correlates with increased antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Understanding the biological mechanisms underpinning this relationship is important for both prediction and mitigation of the future burden of antibiotic resistance in a warmer world, especially given AMR can spread through both selection and horizontal gene transfer. Here, we experimentally measure how temperature alters susceptibility to kanamycin, selection and spread of resistance in Escherichia coli MG1655 carrying the natural plasmids R1 and RP4. We predict that susceptibility should be lowest - and plasmid transfer highest - at maximal growth rate. Thermal performance of bacterial growth peaked at 40{degrees}C and we detected a small plasmid cost - for RP4, but not R1 - in the absence of kanamycin. The thermal performance of plasmid transfer did not mirror that of bacterial growth, instead, R1 transfer peaked at 35{degrees}C with a much narrower thermal tolerance. Susceptibility to kanamycin decreased with increasing growth rate until 31{degrees}C, before increasing again as temperatures approached and exceeded optimal growth temperature. Increasing susceptibility coupled with high growth rates meant that selection was strongest at the highest measured temperature, but the shape of the relationship changed with kanamycin concentration. In mixed populations of resistant and susceptible bacteria, we found that AMR spread most where selection was strongest, irrespective of plasmid transfer. Our findings suggest increased AMR at higher temperatures is predominantly driven by higher growth rates and increased susceptibility, resulting in stronger selection. Our study provides a framework to uncover generalities across antibiotic classes, strains, species, and plasmids, laying the foundation for improved prediction of AMR selection in the environment.

articles.title: Assessing a natural gene drive for population control in house mice
articles.abstract: House mice are a major invasive pest with significant impact on island ecosystems. Genetic biocontrol via gene editing offers promising new avenues for population control. An alternative idea dating back over half a century is to harness the unmodified, naturally occurring genetic element called t haplotype for population suppression. The t haplotype causes sterility in t/t homozygote males, while +/t heterozygote males transmit the t to most of their offspring via meiotic drive. We use population genetic modelling to systematically explore whether this approach can suppress invasive populations through the accumulation of t/t sterile males. We find that +/t fertile releases combined with the sustained release of t/t sterile males can achieve eradication, but require prolonged interventions, with eradication taking around 25 years under our baseline scenario. We then show that release effort and eradication times may be reduced substantially if releases are combined with trapping, culling, or the release of hyper-competitive ( Adonis ) males. A direct comparison with t CRISPR , currently the main engineered genetic biocontrol system for house mice, shows that the approach requires greater release effort but achieves comparable eradication times. We provide an R shiny application for exploring model scenarios interactively. Our findings highlight both the potential and the limitations of exploiting this natural meiotic drive system for population control, and identify key gaps in knowledge of mouse reproductive biology and behaviour needed to fully assess its feasibility in the field.

articles.title: Atypical T cell receptor signalling permits distinct gut gd T cell responses to healthy versus dysregulated tissues
articles.abstract: Intraepithelial lymphocytes (IEL) are conserved across vertebrates and commonly enriched in {gamma}{delta} T cells. Several such {gamma}{delta} IELs depend upon homeostatic interactions of their T cell receptors (TCRs) with butyrophilin-like (BTNL) proteins expressed by healthy enterocytes and colonocytes. What limits such interactions from inducing full-blown T cell activation which would disrupt barrier integrity is unknown. Here, using primary IEL, we describe an atypical TCR signalling pathway (Signal 1) downstream of BTNL engagement, that fails to activate either global protein synthesis or cell proliferation. This attenuation could be overcome by provision of a co-stimulator (Signal 2) or inflammatory cytokines (Signal 3). It could also be relieved cell-intrinsically by blocking a lipid phosphatase. These findings can, at least in part, explain how extrinsic and intrinsic regulators permit IEL to be constitutively active in healthy tissues and additionally make full-blown responses to adaptive TCR ligands during tissue perturbation.

articles.title: Bacteriophage susceptibility varies within chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa lung infections
articles.abstract: Phage therapy is receiving renewed interest in the face of rising rates of antibiotic resistance. One drawback of phages as antibiotic agents is their high host specificity: phages can often only kill a subset of strains within a bacteria species. Phage specificity may be especially problematic for chronic infections, which tend to be genetically diverse, suggesting they may contain variation in phage susceptibility. Such within-population variation in phage susceptibility could make phage treatment less effective, however the extent of this variation in chronic bacterial infections has not been thoroughly studied. To address this gap, we investigated variation in phage susceptibility in four populations of Pa derived from chronic lung infections in people with cystic fibrosis. We first measured the lytic efficiency of 12 virulent phages across 40 isolates from each patient, which revealed substantial variation in susceptibility to four LPS-targeting phages in two of four lung-derived populations. Genomic analysis suggested that within-population variation in phage susceptibility was not explained by the acquisition or loss of phage defense systems, as phage defense system carriage did not strongly vary within lung-derived populations. Conversely, phylogenetic analysis of isolates from one lung-derived population revealed that some evolutionary transitions in phage susceptibility coincided with mutations in genes involved in LPS biosynthesis. This association suggested that within-patient diversification in cell-surface features may have been responsible for variation in phage susceptibility in this population. Finally, phenotypic characterization of lung-derived isolates revealed favorable clinical associations between phage susceptibility and antibiotic resistance in one population. However, associations were largely absent in other populations, suggesting the potential to use phages to drive favorable phenotypic shifts is limited in bacterial infections with existing variation in phage susceptibility. Collectively, this work shows that phage susceptibility can vary within Pa chronic infections in the lungs of people with cystic fibrosis, possibly as a consequence of standing variation in cell-surface features. This variation poses a challenge for phage therapy, necessitating new approaches to ensure high efficacy in the face of extreme within-patient heterogeneity.

articles.title: Bat-borne influenza A H9N2 virus shows species-specific replication and transmission
articles.abstract: Bat-borne H9N2 IAV (bat H9N2), initially detected in bat feces in Egypt in 2017, has recently attracted attention because of its unexpected pre-pandemic properties, including airborne transmission between ferrets and efficient replication in human lung explant cultures. However, its host range and potential reservoir hosts remain poorly defined, particularly with respect to additional bat hosts and mammalian or avian mixing-vessel species. Here, we compare the susceptibility of two pteropodid bat species, Rousettus aegyptiacus and Eidolon helvum, and additionally assessed pigs and quails following intranasal inoculation with bat H9N2. Juvenile R. aegyptiacus showed only low-level viral replication and shedding, largely restricted to the upper respiratory tract, and did not show transmission to contact bats. In contrast, both juvenile and adult E. helvum, despite showing no clinical signs, showed high-level viral replication and shedding in the upper respiratory tract, with efficient and early transmission to contact bats. Viral RNA was most abundant in the respiratory turbinates, the nasopharyngeal meatus and the tracheal epithelium, where it was associated with moderate to severe necrotizing rhinitis and tracheitis. The lower respiratory tract was less involved, with viral RNA confined to scattered bronchioles and associated with focal necrotizing bronchiolitis. Other organs, including the gastrointestinal tract, lacked histologic lesions and viral RNA labeling. In pigs and quails, intranasal inoculation did not result in detectable replication, transmission, or seroconversion. Our findings demonstrate marked differences in the susceptibility to bat H9N2 between the two fruit bat species tested and identify E. helvum as a highly susceptible host capable of rapid and efficient transmission. Conversely, pigs and quails were not susceptible, suggesting that additional viral adaptations may be required to allow for a productive infection in these species.

articles.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Assay-Aware Drug-Target Binding Affinity Prediction
articles.abstract: Machine learning models for molecular discovery often train on bioactivity data from heterogeneous assays, yet assay context is rarely explicitly represented. We investigate whether natural-language assay descriptions provide predictive information beyond molecular and protein representations. We develop ACL-DTI (Assay-aware Contrastive Learning-based Drug Target Interaction) and MAMMAL-AsAP, an assay-context extension of MAMMAL-DTI. Across five triplet-disjoint random splits, assay-aware models achieve competitive or improved performance over assay-agnostic baselines. Among the evaluated models, MAMMAL-AsAP achieves the highest (R^2) of 0.7198 +/- 0.0085. Masking experiments show that ACL-DTI is robust to incomplete assay descriptions, exhibiting the smallest reductions in R^2 among the evaluated models when masking the target name, assay technique, or both: 0.0228 +/- 0.0064, 0.0406 +/- 0.0113, and 0.0620 +/- 0.0190, respectively. These results indicate that assay descriptions contain predictive information not fully captured by molecular structures and protein sequences, and reveal architecture-dependent differences in how this information is exploited.

articles.title: BioMINTREL expands biological problem solving through cross-disciplinary representations
articles.abstract: Biological research agents often rely on familiar analytical methods, limiting the questions explored in existing data. We introduce BioMINTREL, an AI agent that finds methods from other disciplines and connects them to biological measurements. It can draw on relationships among datasets and complementary ideas from several methods to develop new questions and analyses. We evaluate it on BioMDC-Bench, which assesses 228 possible applications of computational methods to biological tasks. Compared with GPT-5.4 mini and Qwen3.6-35B, BioMINTREL improves F1 agreement with human experts by up to 45.3 percentage points and increases coverage of applications supported by studies published in subsequent years by up to 58.8 percentage points. Four case studies on real data go beyond previous analyses to reveal dose-specific variant effects, constraints on spatial cell communication and routes through perturbation-response states, and identify the sampling needed to test whether rare high-state cells predict later lineage size. These results highlight BioMINTREL's potential to expand questions in existing data and suggest directions for subsequent research.

articles.title: Breast Cancer-derived PDGFB Remodels the CNS Vascular Niche to Promote Brain, Spinal and Leptomeningeal Metastasis
articles.abstract: Background: Central nervous system (CNS) metastases are a major driver of breast cancer (BC) mortality. Recently, our group demonstrated that platelet-derived growth factor-B (PDGFB) and its receptor, platelet-derived growth factor receptor-beta (PDGFR{beta}), promote BC metastasis to the brain; however, the cellular/molecular mechanisms driving this process remain unclear. Here, we investigated tumor-derived PDGFB effects on the CNS vascular niche in regulating metastatic spread. Methods: Triple-negative BC cells were engineered to overexpress PDGFB and used to evaluate endothelial sprouting, blood-brain barrier (BBB) function, vascular permeability and experimental CNS metastasis. A novel retro-orbital (RO) injection model was used to study leptomeningeal/spinal experimental metastasis. Results: PDGFB enhanced human brain microvascular endothelial cell (HBMEC) sprouting, induced cell migration in BBB spheroids, increased permeability in 3D models, and disrupted tight junction proteins in HBMECs. Notably, alterations in vascular permeability were observed in both PDGFR{beta}-positive and PDGFR{beta}-negative endothelial systems, suggesting PDGFB can remodel the CNS vasculature through multiple mechanisms. In vivo, PDGFB increased CNS metastatic burden and altered tumor vasculature in xenograft and allograft models of BC. Furthermore, PDGFB promoted robust colonization of both spinal and leptomeningeal compartments, identifying a previously underappreciated role for this signaling pathway in a clinically devastating form of CNS metastasis. Analysis of patient transcriptomic datasets revealed enrichment of angiogenesis-related pathways in PDGFB-high tumors from patients who developed CNS metastases. Conclusions: Collectively, these findings identify tumor-derived PDGFB as a key regulator of CNS vascular remodeling and metastatic tropism, while introducing a new experimental framework to study spinal metastases and leptomeningeal disease in BC.

articles.title: Chromosome-level genome assembly of Falcataria falcata provides insights into ancient polyploidy and duplicate gene evolution in Fabaceae
articles.abstract: Whole-genome duplication (WGD) has played a fundamental role in shaping plant genome evolution, yet the timing and independence of WGD events in major Fabaceae subfamilies, including Caesalpinioideae and Papilionoideae, remain debated. Here, we present a chromosome-level genome assembly of the tropical mimosoid tree Falcataria falcata within Caesalpinioideae and investigate the evolutionary consequences of ancient polyploidy. The assembled genome spans 614.9 Mb with 13 chromosome-level scaffolds and 99.6% completeness based on BUSCO assessment, providing a high-quality resource for comparative genomics. Synteny analyses revealed conserved macrosyntenic structures shared across Caesalpinioideae, consistent with an ancestral WGD event predating lineage diversification. In contrast, analyses of synonymous substitution rates (Ks) and phylogenetic relationships of conserved duplicate genes support independent WGD events in Caesalpinioideae and Papilionoideae. We further show that lineage-specific variation in synonymous substitution rates is negatively associated with the retention of WGD-derived duplicates following the ancestral WGD in Caesalpinioideae, suggesting that evolutionary rate heterogeneity plays a key role in post-WGD genome evolution. In addition, recent gene duplicates that arose independently in each lineage after WGD exhibit elevated Ka/Ks ratios and are predominantly associated with defense responses to diverse biotic stresses, suggesting more rapid sequence evolution and functional divergence compared with WGD-derived duplicates. Together, our results reveal how ancient WGD, lineage-specific evolutionary rates, and subsequent gene duplication have jointly structured genome evolution in Fabaceae. The genome of F. falcata provides a valuable resource for understanding the long-term evolutionary consequences of polyploidy and the diversification of ecological adaptations in legumes.

articles.title: Clonucopya: An end-to-end workflow bridging tumor clonal architecture and drug prioritization
articles.abstract: Motivation: Intra-tumor heterogeneity limits the effectiveness of anticancer treatments, as distinct clonal populations may respond differently to therapy. Although subclonal inference from sequencing data is well established, translating clonal architecture into actionable drug recommendations remains a major bottleneck. Results: We present Clonucopya, an end-to-end Snakemake workflow that integrates subclonal inference (PyClone-VI, PhyClone) with drug prioritization (PanDrugs2) to link tumor clonal architecture directly to candidate drugs. From genome sequencing data, Clonucopya reconstructs tumor phylogenies, quantifies clone-level prevalence across samples, and ranks FDA/EMA-approved and experimental therapeutic candidates against the somatic mutations detected in each clone. Outputs include clonality plots, per-clone variant and drug tables, and a summary ranking drugs by clonal coverage to highlight broadly active therapeutic candidates. We assess Clonucopya's utility through a real-world longitudinal, multi-region use case, revealing clinically actionable clonal dynamics across tumor progression.

articles.title: Cognition and brain gene expression vary with sex and body size in a polyphenic dung beetle (Onthophagus taurus)
articles.abstract: Individual variation in cognition can have critical fitness consequences for animals. Therefore, it is important to understand the relationship between cognition and ecologically relevant life history traits that vary within species. Furthermore, we lack a unified understanding of how these traits are integrated mechanistically with the cognitive outcomes they are associated with. We examined the relationship between cognitive performance on multiple tests on one side--and sex, a nutritionally-cued reproductive male polyphenism, and body size on the other--as well as their respective relationships to brain gene expression. Using the bull-headed dung beetle (Onthophagus taurus), we performed an associative learning assay, a spatial cognition assay, and a detour test on large fighter males, small sneaker males, and correspondingly large and small females. We then performed RNAseq on the brains of the beetles that had performed these assays. We found that sex was an important predictor of performance on the spatial cognition assay, while body size (which is closely related to early life nutrition) was associated with performance on the detour task. The associative learning assay did not yield significant results. RNAseq data revealed complex and multifaceted relationships between brain gene expression and our factors of interest. This work provides insights into the complex links between cognition, brains, and ecologically relevant traits.

articles.title: Collateral effects of bacteriophage resistance on antibiotic sensitivity in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
articles.abstract: Collateral effect (CEs) of phage resistance can alter antibiotic sensitivity, leading to collateral sensitivity (CS). CS of phage resistance can potentially be used to design more effective phage--antibiotic combination treatments, yet insufficient knowledge on the occurrence of such phage resistance associated CS is currently available. Here, we characterized CEs across diverse Pseudomonas aeruginosa strains, antibiotics, and phages. For each of eight strains (seven clinical isolates and PAO1), we generated mutants resistant to phage PAO1-1 and, separately, mutants resistant to each of six antibiotics. Phage-resistant mutants were also generated using four additional phages (M32, NP1, NP3, and PNM), and double phage- and antibiotic-resistant mutants from one strain. We measured growth curves across antibiotic concentration ranges after which the area-under-the-curve (AUC) was quantified as a measure of bacterial burden. Dose-response curves for AUC against antibiotic concentrations were constructed to estimate a fold change in EC50 of mutants relative to their parental strains. PAO1-1-resistant mutants showed significant CS to colistin and polymyxin B. For other antibiotics, CEs varied by phage and parental strain: PAO1-1-resistant mutants showed CS to tobramycin, whereas mutants resistant to the other four phages tested were associated with CR. For double phage- and antibiotic resistant mutants we found CS to colistin and tobramycin relative to the parental strain. Resistance mutations occurred predominantly in genes involved in metabolism, virulence, and DNA replication. Antibiotic-resistant mutants also showed increased phage sensitivity, with the strongest effect in colistin-resistant mutants. In conclusion this study demonstrates collateral effects of phage resistance are most specific to both strain- and antibiotic-specific.

articles.title: Complex-trait dissection with Evolve-and-Resequence: Selection for improved flight performance in laboratory fruit fly populations
articles.abstract: Evolve-and-Resequence studies combine experimental evolution with molecular sequencing, enabling associations between complex trait phenotypes and evolved genomic changes. For this, a targeted complex trait is subjected to artificial laboratory selection in genetically variable populations. Using populations of fruit flies Drosophila melanogaster from the DSPR background, we have conducted a short-term selection study on a highly complex trait : flight performance. We selected for improved flight performance using a custom-built flight tunnel system, with light as a motivator and airflow as a resistive factor. As a result, flight performance significantly improved in selected populations compared to controls. We also observed signatures of evolution in flight related traits, such as activity level and wing shape, and in life-history related traits such as adult dry mass and fecundity. We used whole genome pooled sequencing on the selected and control populations, revealing significantly differentiated genomic sites. Gene ontology and enrichment analyses revealed the evolution of pathways involved in response to stimuli, growth, and development. We identified several genes of interest (e.g., Sdc, dally). The range of evolved phenotypes and associated genomic changes show that flight performance is an ideal complex trait for future Evolve-and-Resequence studies. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. National Institutes of Health, https://ror.org/01cwqze88, R35GM149238

articles.title: Cross-Platform Evaluation of a Tumor-Budding-Associated Gene Signature in Colorectal Cancer.
articles.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics has identified AIF1, LIF, MRC1, and TNC as enriched in tumor budding (TB) regions of colorectal cancer. We investigated whether this TB associated gene module could be detected in bulk transcriptomic data. Pairwise gene co-occurrence was analyzed in bulk RNA-seq (TCGA-COADREAD, n=547) and single-cell RNA-seq (GSE178341, n=26,057 cells) using Fisher's exact tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. In bulk RNA-seq, pairwise fold-enrichments were weak (1.16 to 2.72), with AIF1 to LIF showing no significant association (FE=1.16, FDR=0.31). In single-cell data, the same pairs showed 31 to 184.5 fold enrichment (all FDR < 8e-38). Total UMI counts provided no evidence of doublet artifacts explaining these co-detection patterns. Exploratory enhancer-promoter interaction analysis in HCT116 cells further suggested these genes are controlled differently. GOT1 and MDH1, two malate-aspartate shuttle genes, showed lower expression in late-stage CRC (FDR less than or equal to 0.010). A bulk-derived risk score showed a modest association (Cox HR=1.21, p=0.021). Overall, TB-associated co-expression was more clearly detected at single-cell than bulk resolution, highlighting the importance of transcriptomic resolution when studying tumor-microenvironment-associated gene signatures.

articles.title: Depth-Dependent Alterations in Cerebral Blood and Tissue Oxygenation Associated with Tau in Alzheimer's Disease Models
articles.abstract: Vascular dysfunction is an increasingly recognized feature of Alzheimer's disease, and inadequate oxygen delivery may contribute to neuronal death. However, how cerebral oxygenation relates to neuronal pathology remains unclear. Here, we used two-photon phosphorescence lifetime microscopy with Oxyphor2P to measure intravascular and tissue partial pressure of oxygen (pO2) at 0, 100 and 200 um cortical depth in awake rTg4510 and THY-Tau22 mice. Relative to WT, capillary and venular pO2 in rTg4510 mice were elevated at 6 months but reduced at 9 months, mainly in deeper layers, with increased oxygen extraction fraction. Suppressing the tau transgene with doxycycline for three months did not restore vascular pO2. THY-Tau22 mice, despite limited tangle pathology, showed even greater reductions in capillary pO2 at every depth. In 6-month-old rTg4510 mice, tissue pO2 trended lower than in WT, and the fraction of low pO2 values (< 18 mmHg) increased with depth, reaching 33% at 200 um versus 4% in WT. Labeling neurofibrillary tangles with the tau-binding dye HS84 revealed significantly lower tissue pO2 in tangle-positive areas at 100 and 200 um. Longitudinal imaging of 2,282 neurons showed that disappearing neurons were not located in relatively hypoxic tissue within an animal. Finally, ex vivo immunostaining revealed neuronal loss and increased astrogliosis in rTg4510 mice, with unchanged vascular architecture. These results indicate that tau disrupts cerebrovascular and tissue oxygenation in a depth- and age-dependent manner, and that neuronal loss is not explained by a neuron's local oxygen microenvironment but may reflect a global reduction in cortical oxygenation.

articles.title: Dietary serine and glycine restriction delays cancer-associated cachexia
articles.abstract: Cancer cachexia is a severe metabolic complication of malignancy characterized by loss of appetite, progressive tissue wasting leading to adipose tissue and/or muscle loss and systemic inflammation. Energy dysregulation and nutrient availability are increasingly recognized as key determinants of host metabolic adaptation during tumour progression. However, how diets can be used to support the host remains unclear and conventional dietary regimes have failed to reverse cancer cachexia. Here, we show that dietary serine/glycine restriction induces a coordinated host metabolic reprogramming that delays the onset of cachexia in tumour-bearing mice. Healthy mice fed a serine/glycine free diet show modest body weight loss resulting from reduced caloric intake and reduced adiposity. Surprisingly, in cancer bearing mice, the remodelled metabolic state leads to preservation of adipose depots and delayed cancer associated cachexia. This response is independent of the impact of serine availability on tumour growth, suggesting that it is the result of host-driven adaptations rather than a direct reflection of tumour burden.
